title: City College: students, money and staff
question: How have City College's students, general-fund revenue and spending, and staff moved, and what did its auditors and accreditor say along the way?
finding: City College reported 21,930 full-time-equivalent students in 2015-16, 22,309 at the peak in 2017-18 and 13,508 in 2022-23, while its unrestricted general fund spent $209 million and then $179 million: $9,531 and $13,255 per student. Its year-end balance fell to $8.7 million (5.3% of a year's spending) in 2019-20, the period in which its auditors doubted it could keep operating, and stood at $19.1 million in 2022-23. The federal employment survey counts 1,209 full-time and 1,678 part-time employees in 2017 and 1,039 and 950 in 2025. The college's own reports disagree about 2 of these years' revenue, by as much as $39.2 million.
how: Students, unrestricted general-fund revenue, spending, pay and benefits, and year-end balance are the figures City College itself certified to its accreditor in six annual fiscal reports (2019 to 2024), each covering three years; where a year appears in more than one report the latest report is used and any difference of more than 2% is noted. Staff are from the federal survey of public employment for March of each year. City payments are from the City vendor ledger, leaving out payments coded to the college district's own department and fund. Audit and accreditor findings are on the overseers screen.
limits: These are the unrestricted general fund only, about the part the college controls; grants, bond money and student aid are outside it. The fall in students from 2019-20 coincides with the pandemic. The federal survey marks its 2017 to 2020 staff counts as reported and later years with other codes this project's notes do not explain, so later staff figures may be estimates. The reports for 2015-16 to 2017-18 were revised downward in later filings, so the earliest year may overstate revenue. A college with several sites in a city where living costs are high will cost more per student for honest reasons, and fewer students spread over the same buildings and permanent staff raise the figure without anyone spending more.
